The sequel to the first Witcher game marks a huge departure from its predecessor, and luckily it's mostly for the best. Unlike the previous game, I went into this one knowing that I'd probably have a good time, and I'm glad that turned out to be true.

Clocking in at a little over 35 hours, the Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a little shorter than the first game, even when you complete most of the content on offer. However, this game also doesn't feature as much back and forth between locations as the first one, which is a welcome change. It's still present, some quests even have generous amounts of walking between two characters in a city just to make progress in a quest, but for the most part, quests have been streamlined in that regard. Streamlined, that's a word that could be used to describe this game when comparing it to its predecessor. Some would go as far as to say it has been brutally [i]"consolized"[/i], but I disagree. In fact, I believe it has, in many ways, helped shape this game into a small masterpiece that oozes talent, passion and love from its dev team.

First off, the obvious: This game is downright gorgeous. CD Projekt RED built an entirely new engine for the Witcher 2, and it is a huge improvement on the old Aurora engine they licensed from Bioware for the first Witcher. The trade off for having incredible visuals is that the game has a lot of small buffer zones to camouflage its loading times. To go from Flotsam into the forest, you have to traverse a small area along the walls with two doors that you have to open manually. The same goes for the transition from the Kaedweni camp into the grassy area around it. Vergen has you going through a small corridor before reaching the outside world, and so on. It's no big deal and I'll take this over long loading screens any day, but once you notice it, you'll never be able to ignore it again.

Presentation as a whole has been improved, with a more discrete, less invasive but still tasteful HUD, the menus could be more snappy especially when loading saves but other than that they're fine, character models look superb even if the game sometimes goes too far with the bloom, making faces look weird, and conversations in general are more entertaining, even allowing for the use of signs or intimidation to convince someone. They did however reduce dialog options to just a few words that often don't even represent what your character is going to say, the same thing I blasted Fallout 4 for many times. I really hope this is changed in the third game.

Combat has been improved a LOT, going from [i]"click on your enemy repeatedly, sometimes change your style depending on what enemy you're facing, and spam 360° Igni"[/i] to a system that's somewhat reminescent of Dark Souls at times, with rolls, parries and ripostes, and enemies that pose an actual threat. I also found myself using all the signs at regular intervals, and even potions became a necessity at times, especially while replaying the game on its higher difficulties. It's much more engaging and also feels very rewarding when you learn how to deal with enemies that used to give you a lot of trouble.

Side activites have been expanded to include fist fighting matches and arm wrestling in addition to the returning dice poker. The fist fighting mostly boils down to hitting keys or buttons at the right time, I don't think I ever lost a single match. Arm wrestling has you keeping a circle in a moving bar, which can go wrong and is therefore more engaging, and dice poker is even more luck based than in the first one. These activities can help you earn money but you can never wager much so it still takes ages. Luckily there's mods to increase the max amount of money you can put on the table. The mod support for this games is quite decent and the nexus has many interesting tweaks for players who are looking for a slightly altered experience.

Writing...characters are definitely more interesting and layered than they were in the first game, which was already pretty good at this, but the improved presentation and character models helps taking them seriously now. The overall plot however is not as straightforward as it could be. Even having played the first game and spent an unhealthy amount of time in the lore sections, I still had to print out a map of the world to be sure I knew where exactly countries are in relation to each other. It kind of hurts the enjoyment of a game that's otherwise great at providing entertaining character interactions, quality humor and choices that make you stop and and think, not to mention a huge decision at the end of chapter 1 that literally changes the entirety of chapter 2 and some parts of chapter 3.

Soundtrack and sound design are also an improvement over the first game, making fights more epic and visceral, sad scenes more impactful, all that good stuff. The game offers a lot of replayability. After my first run, I liked it so much that I decided to get all the achievements, so I restarted the game on Dark difficulty, took the alternate path at the end of chapter 1 and discovered a whole new game. And my third playthrough on Insane difficulty also led to some quests I'd never seen before. No section of the game was too tedious to replay, which is a good sign if you ask me.

In conclusion, the Witcher 2 offers a more accessible but not necessarily worse experience than the first game. I prefer the story of the first Witcher, but that aside, pretty much everything else has been improved, from the combat to the visuals, soundtrack, character interactions and quests. I very much recommend playing this game if you like action RPGs, and it's also a great occasion to get into the Witcher series.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is an action role-playing hack and slash video game developed by CD Projekt Red. 

Assassin of Kings continues the story from first game. Once again you play as Geralt of Rivia, a witcher-enhanced and trained humans with special powers who hunt monsters for a living. After saving King of Temeria at the end on The Witcher, Geralt becomes his right-hand man and follows him and his war campaigns, aiding him when possible. During one of those campaigns, King gets assassinated and with his killer disappearing unnoticed, Geralt is left as the only suspect. Now Witcher has to prove his innocence and hunt down kingslayer, while trying to recover lost memories from his previous life. 

Witcher 2 sticks to the gameplay formula from the first game. 
In each Act you will explore different parts of Northern Kingdoms, complete quests, gather experience and improve your arsenal as you progress. 
Quests are seperated on Main Quests that push storyline further, and Secondary Quests where you can do more typical Witcher work, from contracts on monsters to helping random citizens.
There is less quests than first Witcher, but they are longer and feature interesting variety of objectives. Majority of them also has choices, allowing you to complete (or fail) your quests in numerous ways. 

To complete them, you will have to face off different types of human enemies, such as guards, archers, bandits or mages, to monsters you can find in Slavic mythology, classic trolls or gargoyles, different types of vampires or ghosts. Some of them are new, some of the more common ones were already in the first title. 
Combat is more complex. Sword fight remained the same, either you attack swiftly and deal normal damage, or you try a slower, yet heavy hitting attack. Roll or block attacks to avoid damage, and to help yourself you can use Witcher Signs. Set up a trap, throw a fireball, or simply confuse enemies. However new elements include laying down not-magical traps, and ability to aim and throw different types of ranged weapons.
Before combat you can drink potions to improve your statistics and gain an advantage even before the actual fight begun. Preparation is a key to success. 
Combat with new additions and improved previous elements is way, way better than in first game.
While there are still issues, such as locking on the target, enemies having a wonky hit and blocking detection, where sometimes even rolling and stabing them in the back gets magically blocked, and overall movement of Geralt in combat being sluggish, it's still better. 

From missions you earn money, experience and new items.
Orens can be spend in numerous ways. You can use it to play minigames, like dice poker, or (broken) arm-wrestling, to earn even more orens! You can visit few location and have an enjoyable time, or wisely spend it at local merchant to buy everything you need for your next journey. Some missions also involve bribery as a way to progress, so keeping a bit of money in back pocket is a good idea. 

Experience you gather by killing enemies and completing quests, fills up your level meter. After gathering enough, you level up and get one point to spend in your skill paths. 
Game features 4 different paths you can upgrade your Geralt. 
First is a training path in which you need to spend few points to unlock next paths, it focuses on upgrading core abilities. Once you unlock other paths, you can spend rest of your points in any of them. 
Swordsmanship path improves Geralt's sword fighting abilities, unlocking new moves and improving sword stats, magic improves Witcher Signs, from how many you can use to their power, and alchemy which includes perks such as reducing the negative effects of potions or allowing you to drink more of them before the combat. 

Like in RPG's it tends to be, there are plenty of items you find during your quests, some of them can be sold, some of them can be equipped, some of them can be simply used. 
Besides a variety of main and secondary weapons, you can find and equip different parts of outfits that improve your armor and add additional resistance, collect crafting materials for potions and clothing, books, monster trophies, and way more. And if you ever run out of place in your inventory, you can treasure some of your items in a chest, to keep them safe. 

Witcher is a heavy-story driven game, so while combat is a big part of the game, major choices and biggest impact happens in dialogue and writing. With this entry focusing on political issues of Northern Kingdoms and Geralt playing a huge role in the events, it's not really a game for people who focus on slashing things only. No doubt the story, characters, consequences of your actions are the best part of it. Second positive that comes out of this design is replayability of the game. It's one of the games you have to at least play twice, to check out how things go if you pick a second option here and there. Plus mid portion of the game plays out differently depending on what side you will pick.  

While narration is polished, you will find dirt here and there. 
I already mentioned combat issues, and that is where most of them can be noticed.
That's why I'm thankful for a great storyline, as everytime I entered a combat I wanted to stop playing. Not going to repeat myself, but it still needs to be worked on. It's an improvement over first game, but that is not an achievement.
Stealth sections feel unnecessary and are not fun to play, thankfully there are only 2 or 3 of those so it's not a big deal.
Clearly Geralt is not a marathon runner, because story in Assassins of Kings at the last part of the game feels weak. Cliffhanger ending doesn't help.

Now, because this is an "Enhanced Edition" of Witcher 2, it's worth knowing what you get in it. 
EE includes new quests adding around 4 hours of gameplay, arena mode if you want to show off your combat skills, new tutorial, new cinematics in game, including new intro and outro. Plus interface, gameplay, bug fixes and improvements, around 100 of them apparently, but I have not played the "base version" so I can't confirm that. 
Is it worth? Considering it's the only version available on Steam it's not like you have a choice in the first place. 

Performance wise game is fantastic. 
From time to time I had longer loading times but besides that, everything worked smoothly.

More slavic inspired soundtrack is a huge yes in my book! Doesn't matter if you fight for your live, or you wander around the city hearing all the conversations, it's damn well made. 
Voice acting improved, you actually feel like majority of characters can be considered living beings and not robots like in first game. 

Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a great game, and a massive improvement over first title.
Better combat, world and audio design, with still fantastic story filled with hard decisions, and even harder consequences. Why change the formula, when you can simply enhance it? 8/10!

TLDR:  Excellent role-playing game, if a bit challenging.

So, I write this a few months after The Witcher series dropped on Netflix, which seems to have sparked an interest in the series as a whole--which is good, because as a whole, the games are outstanding and Witcher 2 is no exception.

The second tale of Geralt of Rivia opens with him in service to King Foltest of Temeria. Unfolding events end with Geralt being blamed for the king's murder and the game is off and running. The game unfolds in three distinct acts, set in three different areas as Geralt keeps trying to piece his memory together and discover the identity of Foltest's actual killer.

Unlike the first Witcher game, which used a licensed Aurora Engine from Bioware, Witcher 2 was developed with CD Projekt Red's in-house engine, REDEngine, and the difference couldn't be clearer. Character animations are (for the most part) clean, smooth, and natural. Ditto facial expressions. I noticed this best in a scene where several bandits suggest vandalizing a certain relic and one character's face reflects such dismay and disbelief at the idea that I was genuinely impressed. The graphics in general are quite excellent, and an enormous step up from the first game. I think they still hold up well today.

The graphics are also quite bloody. Gameplay and cutscene alike display some rather stark violence, not to mention swearing and nudity. Hookers are available, in vivid detail. Geralt doesn't seem to be the gigolo he was in the first game and the number of possible love interests is less, though the cut scenes of...ahem..."romance" are quite a bit more intense. The (potential) liaison with a certain red-haired sorceress might be the most graphic thing I've seen in a video game that wasn't modded or outright porn from the start. As with the first Witcher, not a game for children.

The overall interface was easy enough to use and pretty simple, though the control scheme is quite a bit different from the first game. The player can select a number of skills from trees that emphasize the character's skill at combat, alchemy, or magic. There are good takeaways from every tree, though depending on the character's play style, some will help more than others. Still no jumping to be seen, so once again, Geralt is stymied by waist-high fences and shrubbery, though climbing short cliffs and ladders integrates smoothly with the character's movement.

Like most good RPGs, choices and consequences matter. Seemingly small choices made early on can have repercussions later in the game. Decisions made in the first act will even affect the flow and location of quests and events in act two and three and there are multiple ways in which this story ends, all based on player choices. Fights can be avoided through dialogue choices (or picked, if the player has a grudge against one of the NPCs) and the consequences for both are there. There is even at least one fight that can be avoided if the player played the first game, made certain decisions, and imported their save file! This branching dialogue/decision tree seems to be something CD Projekt Red is excelling at. The story is excellent and many of the cutscenes are well-executed and gripping.

The voice acting, music, and sound effects are all well done and I scarcely noticed any issues, though Geralt's stock pile of combat catch-phrases quickly grows repetitive.

The combat took some getting used to, especially after the first game. Choices between swift and strong attacks, signs, parrying and dodging, tossing bombs, drinking potions--all those tactics return. But it's significantly harder than the first game. It's not "Dark Souls difficult" but it is quite a bit harder than say, Skyrim. The player must master the art of the dodging roll to evade strikes and on anything other than Easy difficulty, must do it well. Damage taken in the back can drop Geralt in one swing if the foe is strong enough, so constant movement and re-positioning are critical and the player should never, ever let themselves get surrounded. Think tactically, keep Quen (your temporary force field) up, never stop moving, and plan your strikes. Despite the rather unforgiving nature of the combat, I found myself enjoying it and I looked forward to it every time I saw a significant fight coming.

You'll need two at least partial runs to get all the Steam Achievements, since some come from one side of the quest line, and some come from the other. I favored the human side over the elf one; not for solidarity, I just liked the quest flow better. (By the way, if you take the human side and let Hensalt live, you're a better man than me.)  I finished two play-throughs with all but one achievement done, which requires beating the game on the hardest difficulty--with permadeath. Knowing my questionable skill level and how many times I died on Normal, I didn't even try it.

There are a handful of other nitpicks. Sometimes, lining up on an object to loot it requires the player to shuffle around a little until the games "radar" picks it up and highlights it with the interaction button and mis-clicking that button can easily lead the player to exit a building or climb down a ladder when they were trying to pick something up. The dice poker minigame from the first Witcher returns and is equally as annoying--more annoying, actually.

But those are just that: nitpicks. Witcher 2 Enhanced Version is a fun RPG, with consequential choices, a deep multi-layered story, and solid gameplay. It's a few years old but no RPG fan should pass this up.

Pros
- Deep RPG experience
- Good graphics and voice acting
- Exciting combat

Cons
- Going to challenge some players
- Minor movement issues, and no jumping obstacles!

Final Score: 8.5/10

- Before you buy if you've played Witcher 3 and you're thinking of going backwards:

The Witcher 2 isn't necessarily an open-world experience. The game progression is fairly streamlined, sacrificied to an insane amount of player agency throughout the game making subsequent acts into almost a different game altogether - and, of course, that sacrifice also comes with the playtime (one playthrough is going to take you 30-40 hours even with all the side quests).

Lore-wise, I wish this game had more witchering, but since the story is HIGHLY political (and Geralt sure lets us know how much he enjoys that) you'll be more likely fighting far more humanoids than monsters.

Worth playing not just for the experience itself, but also for what exporting a Witcher 2 save could give to your next Witcher 3 playthrough.

Took me just over 70 hours to do a 100% in terms of achievements, including the permadeath difficulty - which is like 2 times less than one full, immersive playthrough of Wild Hunt so you're welcome to making conclusions :D

[h3][i]"My favorite type of magic, [b]Lesbomancy.[/b]" - Skalen, a horny dwarf[/i][/h3]
After enacting his judgment on the Salamandra organization and saving the king from a witcher assassin, Geralt sought to spend his remaining years with his face firmly planted in the majestic bosom of the sorceress Triss Merigold, turned adviser for the king of Temeria, Foltest. But stuff happens, red-haired booba gets abducted, and many people die as a result. The reason? Well, the title of the game pretty much gives you a clue - [i][b]kings die.[/b][/i] But why are heads rolling? I guess that's a mystery only a professional monster slayer can solve.

Personally, I really enjoyed this story more than that of the first game. There was political intrigue, romance, the sex, and lots of revelations for our dear Geraldo. But above that, it's the characters and their personalities that give the story that [i]it[/i] factor. They feel unique, and it's super fun to interact with and listen to their wisdom. My favourite is the furry and the troll couple. Their dialogue was simply gold.

But, [i][b]your decisions also impact the path Geralt's story takes.[/b][/i] And believe me, they actually matter. While the overarching plot is the same, some characters, stories, revelations and events are "gone" depending on what path you walk. This gives the game great replayability, as you won't see everything nor experience the full story with a single playthrough.

[h3][b][i]Bombs away![/i][/b][/h3]
A drastic departure from its predecessor; From automatic attacks with a simple mouse click, stiff movement, combos tied to pressing the left mouse button at the right moment, to the 3rd person action RPG combat many mainstream games employed. [i][b]And, it's decent.[/b][/i] It's too reliant on rolling away and the restricted motionless guard for my liking. And yes, you heard correct - [i][b]you aren't able to move while blocking incoming attacks.[/b][/i] Thus, combat was more challenging because of the poor gameplay decisions made. The stances are also gone, and in their place, we got [i][b]light[/b][/i] and [i][b]heavy attacks.[/b][/i] Disappointing, not gonna lie. The system in the first game provided combat with more depth than simply pressing a light or heavy attack button, with the only difference being how hard you hit.

But, it's not all bad. I liked the way they executed sign combat. It's fast, easy to use, and switching between them doesn't interrupt the flow. They feel more actiony and no longer take half a minute to cast. Prep time is now crucial since [i][b]potions can't be drank mid-combat.[/b][/i] So to come out on top, you must use the bestiary and study your opponent before engaging them. Find their weakness and exploit them. But Geralt can now employ many different bomb variations in his monster-slaying career without needing skill points, which is nice. They can come in clutch when you are getting swarmed, especially those that provide a huge blast.

As for exploration, it's still pretty limited; Each level is a small semi-open area with plenty of NPCs to talk to, play dice with and complete notice board quests. There are a few points of interest in each area, all part of quests, so there is zero chance of you missing them. One new "[i]addition[/i]" is the sporadic stealth segments. They are pretty wonky, and you'll most likely get spotted on your first try. 

The equipment variety greatly improved. Geralt only [i][b]carries two swords,[/b][/i] one for humans, both for [i]monsters[/i]. You can find most of them through quests, but the best ones need a master craftsman who knows how to work a shaft. Besides new weapons, the armour department offers plenty in the way of customization. You can select individual parts that cover your head, shoulders, knees and toes, knees and toes. There are special [i][b]Dark items[/b][/i] tied to the new difficulty in the enhanced edition - [i][b]Dark difficulty.[/b][/i] I really liked them. They inflict passive penalties to your stats if you arent wearing a complete set. Sometimes even with those penalties using them might be beneficial, as they are quite strong. They are costly and require rare material, so wisely spend your hard-earned orens. And lastly, quests. They were excellent. Even the most mundane looking ones were a joy to complete, thanks to the games exceptional writing. I never felt like skipping a quest because they were boring or uninteresting. Each was like a small piece of lore revealed to me, and I simply couldn't get enough.

[h3][i][b]UberSaturation[/b][/i][/h3]
Looking at the time between the first game and this one, it's still mind-blowing what [i]CDPR[/i] achieved in such a short time. They weren't a powerhouse back then, and yet, they built their very own engine, [i]RED Engine[/i], and produced visuals that could rival some of the biggest AAA games at that time. And boy did they melt GPUs in 2011, especially that UberSampleing option. Like, who was that even for? There are some issues tho; Many faces are the same for fodder NPCs, pop-in is very noticeable, not just for textures, but colours as well, on grass most of all. And since it's, well, everywhere, it can be an eyesore. Saturation also seems to be turned to eleven, with colours way too bright at times, making certain situations appear cartoonish. But, the game still holds up great, even with some rough edges here and there. And I prefer its tone to that of the newer entry, [i]The Witcher 3[/i]. [i][b]It feels more gritty.[/b][/i]

The soundtrack and voice acting also improved, especially the latter. I can't even begin to explain how much this impacted my enjoyment of the first game. It felt wooden, emotionless. But here, the voice actors finally made these characters their own. Doug Cockle did an excellent job as Geralt, delivering an "[i]emotionless[/i]" performance. The supporting cast was great as well. Dandelion, Zoltan, Letho and Dethmold were the most noteworthy of the bunch. And with the games improved animations, combining these two produced great cinematic cutscenes. There is one tiny nitpick; Due to their budget, many NPCs had to be voiced by the same person. It wasn't that significant or immersion-breaking for me, but your mileage may vary. As for the soundtrack, it's fine. It's an improvement from the first game, but still, I don't remember many of its tracks. There is some nice combat and ambient music, but nothing that stuck with me, even after three playthroughs.
